title: Hemorrhagic Stroke, Subarachnoid Hemorrhage & Intracranial Pressure
html:
Hemorrhagic stroke requires a different pathway from the ischemic stroke in Lesson 95. Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is bleeding into brain tissue; aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is bleeding into the space around the brain after an aneurysm ruptures. Both can cause rapid neurologic decline, hydrocephalus, or raised intracranial pressure (ICP). The RN's priorities are airway and perfusion, frequent neurologic comparison, prompt imaging and specialist escalation, safe ordered treatment, and prevention of secondary brain injury. Symptoms alone cannot reliably classify a stroke; do not start an ischemic-stroke drug pathway before imaging and team review.

Learning goals

  • Recognize ICH, aSAH, hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, and impending neurologic deterioration.
  • Support anticoagulant reversal and smooth, individualized blood-pressure management for ICH.
  • Explain aneurysm treatment, enteral nimodipine, euvolemia, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) surveillance after aSAH.
  • Apply safe bedside priorities for suspected raised ICP and external ventricular drain (EVD) care.
  • Distinguish evidence-based interventions from routine steroids, prophylactic antiseizure drugs, and indiscriminate fluid or blood-pressure strategies.

First assessment: stabilize and compare

Activate the stroke or neurocritical response for sudden focal weakness, aphasia, severe headache, seizure, vomiting, or reduced consciousness. A thunderclap headache that peaks abruptly is a classic aSAH warning, even if the patient initially remains awake. Assess airway protection, breathing, oxygenation, pulse, blood pressure, glucose, and last-known-well time; arrange urgent head imaging through the local pathway. Obtain a medication history that identifies anticoagulant or antiplatelet name, dose, and last use, plus recent injury and coagulopathy. Record a reproducible neurologic baseline: level of consciousness, orientation or command following, pupils, gaze, limb strength, speech, and focal changes. Glasgow Coma Scale and other validated tools can help trend findings, but a number never replaces a description of what changed.

Escalate a new decline immediately. Falling consciousness, increasing headache or vomiting, new pupil asymmetry, worsening focal deficit, seizure, or new respiratory pattern can indicate expansion, hydrocephalus, seizure, or herniation. Cushing's pattern—hypertension with bradycardia and irregular respirations—is a late, dangerous finding, not a sign to wait for before acting. Reassess airway and hemodynamics, communicate the exact change and time, and prepare for repeat imaging and neurocritical intervention.

Intracerebral hemorrhage: stop expansion and protect perfusion

ICH may occur with chronic hypertension, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, vascular lesions, or anticoagulant exposure. The team evaluates noncontrast CT findings, hemorrhage location and size, intraventricular extension, hydrocephalus, and neurologic trajectory. For anticoagulant-associated ICH, promptly identify the drug and last dose, stop further exposure under the emergency pathway, and prepare the drug-specific prescribed reversal. Warfarin, dabigatran, and factor Xa inhibitors require different strategies; do not assume vitamin K reverses every anticoagulant. Reversal should not wait for a routine handoff when active ICH is suspected or confirmed.

Acute blood-pressure care aims for smooth, sustained control within a clinician-selected target, avoiding large swings and over-lowering that could impair cerebral perfusion. An ICH target is not interchangeable with the permissive-pressure approach sometimes used in ischemic stroke, nor is one numeric goal suitable for every severity. Use an ordered titratable regimen and monitor pressure and neurologic response at protocol intervals. Watch for recurrent bleeding or hematoma expansion, aspiration, fever, glucose disturbances, and venous thromboembolism risk. Intermittent pneumatic compression is used when ordered for immobile patients; stockings alone are not an adequate ICH VTE strategy. Timing of pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis is a team decision after bleeding stability review.

Routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in ICH without seizures does not improve outcomes; treat clinical or electrographic seizures according to orders and consider ordered EEG for unexplained fluctuating consciousness. Routine corticosteroids do not treat ICH-related elevated ICP, and prophylactic continuous hyperosmolar therapy is not a substitute for monitoring and cause-directed care. Platelet transfusion is not routine for a patient taking antiplatelet medication and may cause harm outside selected situations such as emergency surgery or severe thrombocytopenia. Neurosurgical evaluation is urgent for deterioration, cerebellar hemorrhage with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus, or other selected lesions.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: prevent rebleeding and delayed injury

After suspected aSAH, rapid imaging and specialist assessment determine whether a ruptured aneurysm is present. A neurosurgical or endovascular team plans early aneurysm securing by clipping or coiling when appropriate, usually at a center with neurocritical expertise. Before the aneurysm is secured, monitor for rebleeding and support ordered blood-pressure and comfort measures without abrupt, unapproved changes. Hydrocephalus and reduced consciousness may require CSF diversion. After repair, continue frequent neurologic exams: new focal weakness, language change, or decline in alertness can signal DCI and needs immediate evaluation.

Enteral nimodipine is an important aSAH treatment to reduce DCI and improve functional outcome; it is not a reason to give routine IV nimodipine. Verify the ordered route and monitor for hypotension while preserving the treatment plan with the neurocritical team. Maintain prescribed euvolemia and accurate intake-output records; prophylactic hypervolemia or blood-pressure augmentation is not recommended. Symptomatic DCI may require a different team-directed hemodynamic strategy after evaluation. Routine IV magnesium and statins solely to prevent DCI are not recommended. New seizures are treated; blanket antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated for all patients, although selected high-risk cases differ.

Raised ICP and EVD: assess the patient and the system

Brain swelling, an enlarging hematoma, or obstructed CSF flow can raise ICP and reduce cerebral perfusion. A declining level of consciousness is often more useful than waiting for a late vital-sign pattern. Support oxygenation and perfusion; avoid fever, agitation, repeated painful stimulation, and unnecessary delays in treating the cause. Position the head and neck to support venous drainage, commonly with head-of-bed elevation when tolerated and ordered, but reassess blood pressure and perfusion rather than forcing one position for everyone. Hypertonic saline or mannitol may be ordered as a time-limited response to elevated ICP; monitor sodium, osmolality, renal function, fluid status, and neurologic response according to the chosen therapy. Prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation is not routine; emergency ventilation changes require expert direction.

An EVD can drain CSF and permit ICP monitoring when hydrocephalus or selected severe injury warrants it. Follow the unit's exact leveling, drainage height, clamping, transport, and sampling orders. Keep the system closed and aseptic, secure tubing, document CSF color and output, and compare neurologic status with the drainage and pressure trend. A sudden loss of drainage, unexpectedly large drainage, leakage, disconnection, fever, or neurologic decline requires prompt evaluation; do not independently flush, reposition, or change the drain setting. A normal-looking pressure number does not override worsening examination.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify sudden neurologic symptoms, thunderclap headache, medication-related bleeding risk, pupil and consciousness changes, seizure, and perfusion or respiratory instability.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate imaging-confirmed ICH from aSAH and other causes; connect new deficits with expansion, rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizure, DCI, or raised ICP.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Threatened airway, active bleeding, rapidly falling consciousness, obstructive hydrocephalus, and suspected herniation demand immediate help.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare ordered imaging, medication-specific reversal, smooth blood-pressure treatment, aneurysm or neurosurgical evaluation, ICP therapy, and EVD support.
  5. Take action: Activate the appropriate emergency response, carry out orders and neurocritical protocols, protect aspiration and infection safety, and document the timing of every change.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend consciousness, pupils, motor findings, pressure and perfusion, imaging and drain findings, seizures, complications, and rehabilitation needs.

Clinical example

A client taking apixaban develops sudden right-sided weakness and confusion. CT confirms an ICH. The RN reports the exact last apixaban dose, prepares ordered reversal and blood-pressure monitoring, establishes a detailed neurologic baseline, and coordinates transfer to a neurocritical service. When the client becomes harder to arouse and develops a new unequal pupil, the RN immediately escalates for airway reassessment and repeat imaging; a previously stable blood pressure does not make the neurologic decline safe.
